description: Multi-dimensional adversarial review of a diff or capability: correctness, security, and spec compliance, with every finding adversarially verified before it is reported.

findings.title: Concurrent invalidation makes the idle filter throw IllegalStateException, giving a raw 500
findings.evidence: `request.getSession(false)?.let { session -> ... session.getAttribute(LAST_ACTIVITY) ... session.invalidate() ... session.setAttribute(...)` has no guard against a session that another request invalidates in the meantime. After 8 h idle the admin UI usually sends several requests at once on wake or reload. The first request calls `session.invalidate()`. A parallel request that already holds the same session object then calls `getAttribute`/`setAttribute` and Tomcat throws `IllegalStateException: Session already invalidated`. That error escapes the filter chain as a 500 rather than the 401 the spec requires. A sign-out in another tab racing any admin request hits the same path, and so does `signIn`'s `request.getSession(false)?.invalidate()` (AdminSessionController.kt:38).
findings.suggestion: Wrap the session reads and writes (and the invalidate calls in the filter and controller) in a try/catch for IllegalStateException and treat a caught one as 'no session', so the request carries on to the 401 entry point. Add a test that invalidates the session between `getSession(false)` and `getAttribute`.

findings.title: A failed sign-in that carries a valid session resets the idle clock, though the spec says a 401 must not reset anything
findings.evidence: The filter calls `session.setAttribute(LAST_ACTIVITY, now)` for every request that carries an unexpired session, before the outcome is known. `POST /api/admin/session` is `permitAll` and goes through this filter. With a wrong password it returns 401 (`throw InvalidCredentialsException()` at AdminSessionController.kt:36), but the old session keeps its refreshed timestamp. Store spec admin-access, 'Admin session idle timeout': 'A request refused with HTTP 401 SHALL NOT reset anything'. Only CSRF 403s are meant to count as activity.
findings.suggestion: Skip the timestamp update for the sign-in request matcher (successful sign-in sets LAST_ACTIVITY itself), or restore the previous value when sign-in fails. Add a test: signed-in session, wrong-password sign-in 7 h later, then GET 1.5 h after that must return 401.

findings.title: Admin module publishes an unqualified global Clock bean, which the controller injects by type
findings.evidence: `@Bean fun adminClock(): Clock = Clock.systemUTC()` registers a plain `Clock` for the whole context. `AdminSessionController(private val clock: Clock, ...)` (AdminSessionController.kt:24) injects it by type. Later modules (e.g. progress, which needs Europe/Prague weeks) will want a Clock too. They will either silently get the admin module's bean, which crosses the module boundary implicitly (NFR-11), or add a second Clock bean and break the admin controller's injection with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.
findings.suggestion: Inject the bean by name or qualifier (`@Qualifier("adminClock")`) in the controller. Alternatively, move a single application Clock into `shared` as its documented public bean and have admin consume it.

findings.title: The sign-in advice takes over HttpMessageNotReadable and HttpMediaTypeNotSupported handling for the whole app at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE
findings.evidence: `@RestControllerAdvice @Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)` handles these exceptions for every controller. Non-sign-in paths are delegated to a hand-built `object : ResponseEntityExceptionHandler() {}` rather than Boot's `ProblemDetailsExceptionHandler` (enabled by `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled: true`). An admin-module advice now silently decides the 400/415 bodies for the child API too. Any shared advice added later for these exceptions (for example human catalog messages per AGENTS.md) will be shadowed. The sign-in check also relies on an exact `request.requestURI == "/api/admin/session"` match, so a servlet context path would break it.
findings.suggestion: Restrict the advice to the admin controller (`@RestControllerAdvice(assignableTypes = [AdminSessionController::class])`). This catches the body/media-type errors that happen after handler selection. Media-type mismatches during mapping need the URI check kept, but compare against `AdminSessionApi.PATH_SIGN_IN` using `request.servletPath` instead of `requestURI`.

findings.title: Sign-out and expiry don't clear the SESSION cookie in the browser
findings.evidence: `signOut` calls `request.getSession(false)?.invalidate()` and `csrfTokens.saveToken(null, ...)`. That expires XSRF-TOKEN, but no Set-Cookie expires `SESSION` (path `/api/admin`). The idle filter's `session.invalidate()` doesn't clear it either. The browser keeps sending a dead session id. It's harmless server-side, but the stale cookie remains and every later request goes through a failed session lookup.
findings.suggestion: On sign-out (and optionally when the idle filter invalidates), write an expired `SESSION` cookie with the same path, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes. Spring Security's `CookieClearingLogoutHandler` can do this, or you can write the cookie directly.

findings.title: Admin sign-in has no throttling, so a LAN client can guess passwords online without limit and use BCrypt to load the CPU
findings.evidence: POST /api/admin/session is permitAll and has no delay, counter or concurrency cap. Each attempt costs one BCrypt check at the default strength of 10 (AdminCredentials.kt:18, about 100 ms), and Tomcat's worker pool can run many in parallel. A tech-savvy child, or any device on the home Wi-Fi, can script tens of guesses per second against a weak but policy-compliant passphrase (12+ characters, such as a Czech phrase plus digits). The same flood also keeps the laptop's CPU busy. The design lists lockout and rate limiting as non-goals, so this is a recorded, accepted risk. It is flagged only because the checklist asks for brute-force resistance and none exists.
findings.suggestion: Keep the 'no lockout' decision but add something cheap that cannot lock the admin out: a global semaphore of 1–2 concurrent sign-in checks plus a fixed delay of about 1 s after each failure. Alternatively raise the BCrypt strength to 12. If the risk stays accepted, record that in the store spec's risk section so it is not raised again.

findings.title: The admin password and the SESSION cookie travel in cleartext on the home LAN (no Secure flag, no TLS)
findings.evidence: server.servlet.session.cookie sets http-only and same-site but not secure. XSRF-TOKEN is also issued without Secure, and the spec scenario explicitly checks the cookies 'over HTTP'. When the app is reached from another device by its LAN address (NFR-2's RFC 1918 mode), the sign-in body {password} and the SESSION cookie are sent unencrypted. Any device on the same Wi-Fi, such as a guest's phone, a compromised IoT device or a passive sniffer, can capture the admin password or replay the session for up to 8 h of idle time. Then it can mutate content once slices 5–9 add admin handlers. In the default 127.0.0.1 binding this does not apply.
findings.suggestion: Document LAN mode as 'trusted network only', or terminate TLS in the frontend nginx (for example a self-signed or mkcert certificate for the LAN IP). Then set server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true and add .secure(true) in the CSRF cookie customizer. Both can be gated on a DOUCKO_TLS flag so localhost dev still works.

findings.title: The build has no Maven dependency advisory scan, so checklist item 7 cannot be verified
findings.evidence: The build plugins are spring-boot, openapi-generator, build-helper, kotlin, failsafe, jacoco and spotless. There is no OWASP dependency-check, OSV-Scanner or similar step, and qa:verify does not run one. This slice adds Spring Security session and CSRF code to the attack surface, but nothing in the repo reports critical or high CVEs in spring-security, tomcat-embed or jackson. This review could not produce an advisory list with exploitability notes from repo evidence.
findings.suggestion: Add a scan step to qa:verify, for example `osv-scanner --lockfile pom.xml` or the org.owasp dependency-check-maven plugin with failBuildOnCVSS=7. Commit its report next to docs/qa/automated-verification-latest.md so the dependency item has evidence.

findings.title: Coverage summary: 39 backend-owned scenarios: 37 implemented, 2 partial, 0 missing, 0 contradicted
findings.evidence: I checked the store spec admin-access (authentication, child endpoints, cookie+CSRF, idle timeout, no lockout, password policy) and the delta's 5 scenarios against AdminSessionTest, AdminIdleTimeoutTest, AdminSessionIT, AdminStartupTest, AdminPasswordPolicyTest and AdminCredentialsTest. These scenarios are implemented and tested: 401-before-403 (AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:135-139), SESSION cookie path /api/admin (application.yaml:39), idle filter (AdminIdleTimeoutFilter.kt:27-35), 72-byte full compare (AdminCredentials.kt:294-298) and the startup policy (AdminPasswordPolicy.kt:320-326). The only gaps are the two child-endpoint scenarios listed below. The frontend-owned scenario 'Admin UI shows sign-in without a session' is excluded.
findings.suggestion: No action. This entry only carries the coverage line.

findings.title: 'Child write is limited to its own practice' is deferred to slice 7 but nothing tracks it there
findings.evidence: Store scenario: 'WHEN the child submits POST /api/child/missions/{missionId}/tasks/{taskId}/attempts with ... "accepted":["99"] ... THEN ... graded against 12, not 99 AND GET /api/admin/tasks/{taskId} afterwards returns prompt P...'. Code reality: there is no attempt endpoint and no test. The deferral appears only in design.md:11-13 ('It is proven in slice 7'). tasks.md does not mention it, and nothing ties this scenario to slice 7's implement-practice-flow-api.
findings.suggestion: Record the deferral where it will be enforced. Add a carried-over task or acceptance-contract entry (trace/acceptance-contracts.json) so implement-practice-flow-api must test this scenario, and note it as 'Scope NOT delivered' in current-state.md.

findings.title: 'No content-changing child operation exists' has no executable check in the backend
findings.evidence: Scenario: 'WHEN the operations under /api/child/** in api/openapi.yaml are listed THEN none of them creates, updates or deletes a source, task, mission, answer spec, hint, translation or image'. No test in src/test lists the generated Child*Api operations. Child-side NFR-1 is enforced only structurally: the shared chain is permitAll, stateless and has no CSRF (SecurityConfiguration.kt diff).
findings.suggestion: Add a test that reflects over the generated cz.doucko.api child interfaces (or parses contract/api/openapi.yaml) and asserts that no /api/child operation targets content resources. Alternatively, state in the spec or plan that the docs store owns this scenario.

findings.title: XSRF-TOKEN cookie gets SameSite=Strict, which no spec or contract mentions
findings.evidence: Delta spec: 'The XSRF-TOKEN cookie SHALL be readable by scripts (no HttpOnly) and scoped to /'. openapi.yaml:312 says only '`XSRF-TOKEN` (readable by JS, sent back as X-XSRF-TOKEN)'. Code: `setCookieCustomizer { it.sameSite("Strict") }`. Sign-out also clears the token (AdminSessionController.kt signOut → saveToken(null)), which is also unspecified.
findings.suggestion: Add the SameSite=Strict attribute and the clear-on-sign-out behaviour to the delta's 'Session cookie scope' requirement (and to the openapi Set-Cookie description in a docs-store change), then cover both in AdminSessionIT.

The file was updated in this diff, but it says 'Active change: `implement-admin-access-api` (slice 2, branch `slice2-admin-access`, not committed)' and '(uncommitted)' (line 20). findings.title: New module `cz.doucko.admin` is not in the declared modular-monolith module list
findings.evidence: AGENTS.md (NFR-11) lists modules as 'content, checking, practice, progress, tutor, storage, shared'. This slice adds a new top-level module `cz.doucko.admin` (design.md decision 1, 'Own module, own chain') and makes shared SecurityConfiguration defer /api/admin/** to it.
findings.suggestion: Amend the module list (docs-store ../docs/factory or an ADR under docs/adr/) to include `admin`, so the NFR-11 module boundary documentation matches the code. Do not edit installed files directly.

findings.title: The startup-refusal scenario is verified at context level, not as a process exit status
findings.evidence: Store scenario 'Short password': 'THEN it exits with a non-zero status before serving any request'. The test asserts that the application context fails to start and that the message names ADMIN_PASSWORD/12 and omits the value. Nothing asserts the non-zero process exit, although Spring Boot normally exits non-zero on context failure. The compose smoke (docs/qa/evidence/slice2-compose-smoke.md) covers only a valid password.
findings.suggestion: Accept context failure as the mechanism and say so in design.md, or add one compose or process-level smoke step that starts the backend with an 11-character ADMIN_PASSWORD and records the non-zero exit.

result.reasoning:
The mechanism is real. The app uses plain Tomcat container sessions: there's no spring-session dependency, `server.servlet.session` is set in application.yaml, and the security context comes from HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository. Tomcat's StandardSession `getAttribute`, `setAttribute` and `invalidate` all throw `IllegalStateException` ("... Session already invalidated") once the session is invalid. AdminIdleTimeoutFilter.kt:27-34 has no guard. If request B gets the session from `getSession(false)` and request A then calls `invalidate()` (idle expiry in the filter, signOut at AdminSessionController.kt:53, or signIn at :38) before B reaches line 29, 31 or 33, B throws. The exception escapes the filter, so the request ends up as a 500 instead of a 401.

The impact is overstated, though. Tomcat's `Request.doGetSession` checks `isValid()`, so any request that calls `getSession(false)` after A has invalidated gets null and goes cleanly to the 401. Only a request that fetched the session object in the microseconds before A's `invalidate()` and touches it afterwards can hit this. "Several requests on wake" mostly doesn't trigger it.

The same race exists downstream in Spring Security's HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository, which also calls `getAttribute` without a guard. So this is a general servlet-session race, not something specific to this filter, and wrapping only this filter won't fully remove it.

Verdict: the bug is genuine, but the window is very narrow and it's mostly framework-level, so I'm confirming it and downgrading it from major to minor.

The mechanism is real. pom.xml has no Spring Session, Jetty or Undertow, so the app uses Tomcat's own StandardSession. In Tomcat, `getSession(false)` checks `isValid()` only once, when the call is made. After that, `StandardSession.getAttribute`, `setAttribute` and `invalidate` each throw `IllegalStateException` ("Session already invalidated") if the session has become invalid in the meantime. Nothing guards against this. AdminIdleTimeoutFilter.kt:27-34 has no try/catch, and neither does AdminSessionController.kt:38/53. No advice or error handler in src/main deals with ISE either. The filter is added before SecurityContextHolderFilter, so the exception escapes as a 500 from the error path.

It is reachable. Two requests carrying the same expired session can both read `last > idle`; one invalidates and the other's `invalidate()` throws. A sign-out racing another request does the same.

Why I downgrade:
1. The race window is microseconds: between `getSession(false)` and the next session call in the same thread. The admin UI firing several requests at once on wake makes it possible but rare.
2. Only the single authenticated admin can trigger it, and only against their own session. An attacker gets nothing from it: no bypass, no data leak, and the session still ends up invalidated. The worst result is that one parallel request returns 500 instead of 401, and a retry gives the right answer.
3. Spring's own HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository and CSRF session handling have the same generic servlet race, so this is not unique to this code.

It does technically break the "no raw 500" rule and the 401 the spec requires, so it isn't refuted. But it is a low-probability robustness issue (minor), not a major correctness bug. The suggested fix is cheap and reasonable: catch ISE and treat it as 'no session'.

The code does what the finding says. In AdminIdleTimeoutFilter.kt:27-34, any request that has an unexpired session gets `LAST_ACTIVITY = now` before the chain runs. The filter is added to the admin chain (AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:84), and that chain also handles the sign-in matcher (`authorize(signIn, permitAll)` at :73; CSRF is skipped for it at :80). So a wrong-password `POST /api/admin/session` sent with a still-valid session cookie updates the old session's timestamp. Then AdminSessionController.kt:36 throws InvalidCredentialsException and the response is a 401. Nothing restores the earlier value. The 'session invalidated, new timestamp set' code at :38-39 only runs on success.

Spec check (contract/openspec/specs/admin-access/spec.md:192): 'A request refused with HTTP 401 SHALL NOT reset anything'. Read literally, this covers a wrong-password 401, so the finding stands.

Why I'm downgrading: the requirement contradicts itself for this exact case. Line 189-190 says 'Every request that carries a valid, unexpired session cookie SHALL reset the idle clock'. A failed sign-in that carries a valid session matches that sentence, and the code follows it. The 401 sentence seems aimed at requests with no session or an expired one ('SHALL NOT revive an expired session'), not at credential failures. The security impact is also nil. Whoever holds the session cookie can already reset the clock with any GET that succeeds, so a failed sign-in gives them no extra power to extend the session. The mechanism is real and the literal spec text is violated, but treat this as a spec ambiguity to settle in the docs store (say which rule wins for a sign-in 401) more than a real defect. If the 401 rule wins, the suggested fix (skip the timestamp update for the sign-in matcher) is correct.

The mechanism is real. AdminIdleTimeoutFilter.kt:27-34 stamps LAST_ACTIVITY on every request that carries an unexpired session. The admin chain uses securityMatcher("/api/admin/**") and adds the filter before SecurityContextHolderFilter (AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:71,84), and sign-in is both permitAll and CSRF-exempt (lines 73,80). So a POST /api/admin/session with a valid cookie and a wrong password refreshes the timestamp, and AdminSessionController.kt:36 then throws a 401 without touching the session.

Whether this is a defect depends on the spec, and the spec does not support the finding's reading. contract/openspec/specs/admin-access/spec.md:189-192 first says "Every request that carries a valid, unexpired session cookie SHALL reset the idle clock — including a request refused with HTTP 403...". It then says "A request refused with HTTP 401 SHALL NOT reset anything and SHALL NOT revive an expired session." Read in context, and given the scenario at line 198-200 ("8 h 1 min ago → 401 and nothing changes"), the 401 clause covers requests refused because the session is missing or expired. A wrong-password sign-in carrying a valid session is exactly what the first, mandatory sentence covers. The code follows that sentence, and the filter's KDoc says so on purpose. At most the spec is ambiguous; the code does not clearly violate it.

From an exploitability angle, nobody is harmed:
- To extend the session, an attacker must already hold the admin session cookie, which grants full admin access anyway. Refreshing the idle clock gives them nothing new.
- A CSRF-style cross-site POST can't do it either. SameSite cookie rules and the JSON body limit this, and even a successful cross-site POST only extends the legitimate admin's own session. It discloses nothing and changes no data.
- The real admin UI only shows the sign-in form after the session check returns 401, which means the session is already gone. So this path doesn't come up in normal use.

The behavior can be reproduced by hand with curl, but it is not an exploitable or user-visible defect. It is a spec-wording ambiguity at most. If the spec author really meant that failed sign-ins don't count as activity, that should be clarified in the docs store first (a spec change). It should not be filed as a code bug here.

Nothing is wrong with the code as it stands; the finding describes a possible future problem. Today the context has exactly one `java.time.Clock` bean: `adminClock()` at AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:43. A grep of src/main finds no other Clock bean, so `AdminSessionController(clock: Clock)` and the filter-chain parameter `adminClock: Clock` both resolve to it with no ambiguity.

Each failure the finding names depends on code that doesn't exist yet:
1. NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException only happens if some future module adds a second Clock bean that isn't @Primary. That module would be the one introducing the conflict, and it can't be written yet.
2. The NFR-11 boundary claim doesn't hold. Spring Modulith's `verify()` checks type dependencies between application-module packages. `java.time.Clock` is a JDK type, not an admin-module type, so a progress bean that injected a Clock would not depend on `cz.doucko.admin` and verify() would not flag it.

The suggested fix would also hurt the current tests. `AdminWebTestBeans` (AdminWebTestSupport.kt:32-34) replaces the clock with a `@Primary` `MutableClock`, and the controller's injection by type is what lets that test clock reach it. Putting `@Qualifier("adminClock")` on the controller would bypass the @Primary test clock. The controller would then run on the real system UTC clock while the idle-timeout filter used the test clock, which breaks the time-dependent session tests' setup.

This is at most a design or maintainability note: the bean could move to `shared` later. It is not a correctness defect in this code.

The finding describes something that might go wrong later. In the current code it cannot happen. A grep of src/main finds exactly one Clock bean, `adminClock()` at AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:43. Its only consumers are AdminSessionController (by type), the admin filter chain (parameter `adminClock`) and AdminIdleTimeoutFilter (built by hand with that bean). No other module defines or injects a Clock today, so the controller cannot get the wrong bean and there is no NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.

The failure the finding predicts would not be silent either. If a later module added a second, non-@Primary Clock, the context would fail at startup. The by-type injection into the controller's `clock` parameter would hit NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, and every *IT test would catch it at once. It would never reach a user. Spring's parameter-name fallback would still resolve `adminClock` in the filter-chain method.

The test suite already exercises having two Clock beans. AdminWebTestBeans registers a `@Primary` MutableClock next to adminClock, and the context starts and injects correctly. That shows the standard way to resolve it.

The point that "a later module would silently get the admin module's bean" is also speculative. It is a design and modularity concern (NFR-11 / Modulith would flag a cross-module dependency), not a correctness defect that a user or attacker can trigger. Nothing here is reachable, so it is at most a maintainability nit about bean scoping.

The facts in the finding check out, but nothing behaves incorrectly today.

What the code does (SignInFailureAdvice.kt:25-49): it is a global `@RestControllerAdvice` with `@Order(HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)` and no `assignableTypes` or `basePackages` restriction. It handles `HttpMessageNotReadableException` and `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` for every controller. Requests that are not sign-in go to a hand-built `object : ResponseEntityExceptionHandler() {}`. The sign-in check is an exact match `request.requestURI == "/api/admin/session"`. So the claim that it takes over this handling for the whole app is accurate.

Why there is no bug now:
1. Same output as Boot. Boot's `ProblemDetailsExceptionHandler` is itself an empty subclass of `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`. This code sets the MessageSource on its copy, and Boot sets one on its bean the same way (the class implements MessageSourceAware). So child-API 400/415 responses are the same either way.
2. Nothing is shadowed yet. A grep of src/ finds no other `@ControllerAdvice` or `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`.
3. No context path. application.yaml has no `server.servlet.context-path`, so the `requestURI` match works as deployed.

What is left is a design and maintainability risk:
- A shared advice added later for these two exceptions would be silently overridden because this one runs first.
- The admin module owns a cross-cutting concern that belongs in `shared`.
- A context path added later would break the sign-in match.

These risks are real and the suggested fix is reasonable: narrow the advice's scope, and match on `servletPath` against a constant. But the correctness claim depends on future changes, so I'm keeping the finding (not refuted) and downgrading it to a maintainability nit.

The structural description is accurate. `SignInFailureAdvice.kt:25-49` is a global `@RestControllerAdvice` at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE, and it handles HttpMessageNotReadable and HttpMediaTypeNotSupported for every controller. But a real user or attacker cannot hit any problem today:

1. **Same behaviour off sign-in.** On every other path the advice calls `object : ResponseEntityExceptionHandler() {}.handleException(...)` with the app's MessageSource. Boot's `ProblemDetailsExceptionHandler` is an empty subclass of `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`, and Spring also gives it the MessageSource through MessageSourceAware. So the 400 and 415 RFC 7807 bodies for child and other endpoints match what Boot would have returned. A client sees nothing different.
2. **No context path.** `application.yaml` sets no `server.servlet.context-path`; a grep for context-path finds nothing. So `requestURI == "/api/admin/session"` matches the real sign-in path, and the context-path failure is hypothetical.
3. **No advice is shadowed.** There is no other `@ControllerAdvice` or `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` in `src/`. The "future shared advice will be shadowed" point is about future maintainability, not a defect that can be reproduced now.
4. **Not a security issue.** The sign-in branch only turns 400/415 into the same 401 the contract requires, and it applies only to POST on the exact path. Nothing leaks, and an attacker can't use it to get a different response.

What remains is a design and coupling concern (an admin-module advice owns app-wide handlers), not a correctness bug that can occur. With no observable mechanism, this is refuted. At most it is a nit or refactor suggestion.

The mechanism is real. The session is a plain Tomcat container HttpSession configured in `application.yaml:27-39` (`server.servlet.session.cookie.name: SESSION`, path `/api/admin`). It is not Spring Session, so no cookie serializer exists that would write an expiring cookie on invalidate. Tomcat's `HttpSession.invalidate()` sends no Set-Cookie to expire `JSESSIONID`/`SESSION`. `AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:83` has `logout { disable() }`, so Spring Security adds no `CookieClearingLogoutHandler` either. `signOut` (`AdminSessionController.kt:51-57`) only invalidates the session and clears the CSRF cookie through `csrfTokens.saveToken(null, ...)`. Nothing expires `SESSION`, and the idle filter's invalidate behaves the same way. So the browser does keep the dead session id.

It is still not a correctness defect against the contract. The store spec scenario "Sign-out ends the session" (`contract/openspec/specs/admin-access/spec.md:85-90`) only requires that a later GET with the old cookie returns 401, and it does. The stale id can't be revived, and the next sign-in replaces it with a new id. The cost the finding cites, a "failed session lookup", is a single in-memory map miss in Tomcat's session manager. That is negligible. The claim is accurate but cosmetic, closer to a nit than a minor issue.

The mechanism is real, but it has no consequence a real user or attacker can reach. Code facts: there's no Spring Session, just plain Tomcat sessions (`server.servlet.session.cookie.name: SESSION`, path `/api/admin`, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, no max-age). `signOut` (AdminSessionController.kt:53) and AdminIdleTimeoutFilter.kt:31 call `HttpSession.invalidate()`. Tomcat doesn't send an expiring Set-Cookie on invalidate, so the browser does keep the dead `SESSION` id. That part of the finding is accurate.

Why it isn't a problem:
1. Security: the id is invalidated on the server and Tomcat won't bring it back. AdminSessionIT.kt:88 shows a request with the old cookie after sign-out gets 401. AdminIdleTimeoutTest checks that requests after expiry don't revive the session. A stolen copy of the stale cookie is worthless.
2. Functionality: the next sign-in calls `getSession(true)`, which creates a new id and sends a fresh Set-Cookie that overwrites the stale one (same name and path). A request without a session also gets the same 401 problem response, so the leftover cookie changes nothing the user sees.
3. The "every later request goes through a failed session lookup" cost is a single map miss in Tomcat's in-memory manager. It only happens on `/api/admin` paths, because of the cookie path, and is negligible.
4. It's a browser-session cookie with no max-age, so it disappears when the browser closes. It holds no PII. The finding itself says it's "harmless server-side."

There's no exploit or reproducible user-facing failure, so this is cosmetic hygiene at most. If it's kept, it should be a nit, not a correctness defect.

confirmed.evidence: `request.getSession(false)?.let { session -> ... session.getAttribute(LAST_ACTIVITY) ... session.invalidate() ... session.setAttribute(...)` has no guard against a session that another request invalidates in the meantime. After 8 h idle the admin UI usually sends several requests at once on wake or reload. The first request calls `session.invalidate()`. A parallel request that already holds the same session object then calls `getAttribute`/`setAttribute` and Tomcat throws `IllegalStateException: Session already invalidated`. That error escapes the filter chain as a 500 rather than the 401 the spec requires. A sign-out in another tab racing any admin request hits the same path, and so does `signIn`'s `request.getSession(false)?.invalidate()` (AdminSessionController.kt:38).
confirmed.suggestion: Wrap the session reads and writes (and the invalidate calls in the filter and controller) in a try/catch for IllegalStateException and treat a caught one as 'no session', so the request carries on to the 401 entry point. verifierNotes:
The mechanism is real. The app uses plain Tomcat container sessions: there's no spring-session dependency, `server.servlet.session` is set in application.yaml, and the security context comes from HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository. Tomcat's StandardSession `getAttribute`, `setAttribute` and `invalidate` all throw `IllegalStateException` ("... Session already invalidated") once the session is invalid. AdminIdleTimeoutFilter.kt:27-34 has no guard. If request B gets the session from `getSession(false)` and request A then calls `invalidate()` (idle expiry in the filter, signOut at AdminSessionController.kt:53, or signIn at :38) before B reaches line 29, 31 or 33, B throws. The exception escapes the filter, so the request ends up as a 500 instead of a 401.

The impact is overstated, though. Tomcat's `Request.doGetSession` checks `isValid()`, so any request that calls `getSession(false)` after A has invalidated gets null and goes cleanly to the 401. Only a request that fetched the session object in the microseconds before A's `invalidate()` and touches it afterwards can hit this. "Several requests on wake" mostly doesn't trigger it.

The same race exists downstream in Spring Security's HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository, which also calls `getAttribute` without a guard. So this is a general servlet-session race, not something specific to this filter, and wrapping only this filter won't fully remove it.

Verdict: the bug is genuine, but the window is very narrow and it's mostly framework-level, so I'm confirming it and downgrading it from major to minor.

The mechanism is real. pom.xml has no Spring Session, Jetty or Undertow, so the app uses Tomcat's own StandardSession. In Tomcat, `getSession(false)` checks `isValid()` only once, when the call is made. After that, `StandardSession.getAttribute`, `setAttribute` and `invalidate` each throw `IllegalStateException` ("Session already invalidated") if the session has become invalid in the meantime. Nothing guards against this. AdminIdleTimeoutFilter.kt:27-34 has no try/catch, and neither does AdminSessionController.kt:38/53. No advice or error handler in src/main deals with ISE either. The filter is added before SecurityContextHolderFilter, so the exception escapes as a 500 from the error path.

It is reachable. Two requests carrying the same expired session can both read `last > idle`; one invalidates and the other's `invalidate()` throws. A sign-out racing another request does the same.

Why I downgrade:
1. The race window is microseconds: between `getSession(false)` and the next session call in the same thread. The admin UI firing several requests at once on wake makes it possible but rare.
2. Only the single authenticated admin can trigger it, and only against their own session. An attacker gets nothing from it: no bypass, no data leak, and the session still ends up invalidated. The worst result is that one parallel request returns 500 instead of 401, and a retry gives the right answer.
3. Spring's own HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository and CSRF session handling have the same generic servlet race, so this is not unique to this code.

It does technically break the "no raw 500" rule and the 401 the spec requires, so it isn't refuted. But it is a low-probability robustness issue (minor), not a major correctness bug. The suggested fix is cheap and reasonable: catch ISE and treat it as 'no session'.

rejected.title: Admin module publishes an unqualified global Clock bean, which the controller injects by type
rejected.evidence: `@Bean fun adminClock(): Clock = Clock.systemUTC()` registers a plain `Clock` for the whole context. `AdminSessionController(private val clock: Clock, ...)` (AdminSessionController.kt:24) injects it by type. Later modules (e.g. progress, which needs Europe/Prague weeks) will want a Clock too. They will either silently get the admin module's bean, which crosses the module boundary implicitly (NFR-11), or add a second Clock bean and break the admin controller's injection with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.
rejected.suggestion: Inject the bean by name or qualifier (`@Qualifier("adminClock")`) in the controller. Alternatively, move a single application Clock into `shared` as its documented public bean and have admin consume it.
verifierNotes:
Nothing is wrong with the code as it stands; the finding describes a possible future problem. Today the context has exactly one `java.time.Clock` bean: `adminClock()` at AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:43. A grep of src/main finds no other Clock bean, so `AdminSessionController(clock: Clock)` and the filter-chain parameter `adminClock: Clock` both resolve to it with no ambiguity.

Each failure the finding names depends on code that doesn't exist yet:
1. NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException only happens if some future module adds a second Clock bean that isn't @Primary. That module would be the one introducing the conflict, and it can't be written yet.
2. The NFR-11 boundary claim doesn't hold. Spring Modulith's `verify()` checks type dependencies between application-module packages. `java.time.Clock` is a JDK type, not an admin-module type, so a progress bean that injected a Clock would not depend on `cz.doucko.admin` and verify() would not flag it.

The suggested fix would also hurt the current tests. `AdminWebTestBeans` (AdminWebTestSupport.kt:32-34) replaces the clock with a `@Primary` `MutableClock`, and the controller's injection by type is what lets that test clock reach it. Putting `@Qualifier("adminClock")` on the controller would bypass the @Primary test clock. The controller would then run on the real system UTC clock while the idle-timeout filter used the test clock, which breaks the time-dependent session tests' setup.

This is at most a design or maintainability note: the bean could move to `shared` later. It is not a correctness defect in this code.

The finding describes something that might go wrong later. In the current code it cannot happen. A grep of src/main finds exactly one Clock bean, `adminClock()` at AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:43. Its only consumers are AdminSessionController (by type), the admin filter chain (parameter `adminClock`) and AdminIdleTimeoutFilter (built by hand with that bean). No other module defines or injects a Clock today, so the controller cannot get the wrong bean and there is no NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.

The failure the finding predicts would not be silent either. If a later module added a second, non-@Primary Clock, the context would fail at startup. The by-type injection into the controller's `clock` parameter would hit NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, and every *IT test would catch it at once. It would never reach a user. Spring's parameter-name fallback would still resolve `adminClock` in the filter-chain method.

The test suite already exercises having two Clock beans. AdminWebTestBeans registers a `@Primary` MutableClock next to adminClock, and the context starts and injects correctly. That shows the standard way to resolve it.

The point that "a later module would silently get the admin module's bean" is also speculative. It is a design and modularity concern (NFR-11 / Modulith would flag a cross-module dependency), not a correctness defect that a user or attacker can trigger. Nothing here is reachable, so it is at most a maintainability nit about bean scoping.

rejected.title: XSRF-TOKEN cookie gets SameSite=Strict, which no spec or contract mentions
rejected.evidence: Delta spec: 'The XSRF-TOKEN cookie SHALL be readable by scripts (no HttpOnly) and scoped to /'. openapi.yaml:312 says only '`XSRF-TOKEN` (readable by JS, sent back as X-XSRF-TOKEN)'. Code: `setCookieCustomizer { it.sameSite("Strict") }`. Sign-out also clears the token (AdminSessionController.kt signOut → saveToken(null)), which is also unspecified.
rejected.suggestion: Add the SameSite=Strict attribute and the clear-on-sign-out behaviour to the delta's 'Session cookie scope' requirement (and to the openapi Set-Cookie description in a docs-store change), then cover both in AdminSessionIT.
verifierNotes:

1. **The change's own design records both behaviours.** `openspec/changes/implement-admin-access-api/design.md:36-40`, decision 5, says: "`CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse()` with cookie path `/` and SameSite=Strict … Sign-in is excluded and issues a fresh token. Sign-out deletes it." So SameSite=Strict and clearing the token on sign-out were deliberate, documented choices, not unplanned drift.

2. **A test already covers it.** `AdminSessionIT.kt:71` asserts `xsrf shouldContain "SameSite=Strict"` against a real HTTP response. The compose smoke evidence (`docs/qa/evidence/slice2-compose-smoke.md:13`) also shows `XSRF-TOKEN (Path=/; SameSite=Strict)`. The suggestion to "cover both in AdminSessionIT" is at least half done already.

3. **Nothing contradicts the spec.** The delta spec (`spec.md:28-29`) requires the cookie to be readable by scripts (no HttpOnly) and scoped to `/`. The code meets both, and nothing in the spec forbids a SameSite attribute. The openapi text, "readable by JS, sent back as X-XSRF-TOKEN", still holds: the admin UI is same-site, so a Strict cookie is still sent and readable. NFR-15 and OQ-23 call for SameSite=Strict on the admin session, and the CSRF cookie follows the same policy. That is consistent hardening.

4. **Deleting the token on sign-out is consistent too.** The session is invalidated at that point, and the next sign-in issues a fresh token, so it breaks no specified flow.

rejected.title: The startup-refusal scenario is verified at context level, not as a process exit status
rejected.evidence: Store scenario 'Short password': 'THEN it exits with a non-zero status before serving any request'. The test asserts that the application context fails to start and that the message names ADMIN_PASSWORD/12 and omits the value. Nothing asserts the non-zero process exit, although Spring Boot normally exits non-zero on context failure. The compose smoke (docs/qa/evidence/slice2-compose-smoke.md) covers only a valid password.
rejected.suggestion: Accept context failure as the mechanism and say so in design.md, or add one compose or process-level smoke step that starts the backend with an 11-character ADMIN_PASSWORD and records the non-zero exit.
verifierNotes: The behaviour is correct; the finding only points to a small gap in test evidence. `DouckoBackendApplication.kt:9-11` is a plain `fun main` that calls `runApplication<DouckoBackendApplication>(*args)`, with no try/catch, no custom `SpringApplication` setup and no exit-code override. If the `AdminCredentials` bean rejects `ADMIN_PASSWORD` at startup, Spring Boot's `SpringApplication.run` reports the failure, closes the context and rethrows. The exception leaves `main` uncaught, so the JVM exits non-zero, and no request is served because the web server starts only after the context refreshes. `AdminStartupTest.kt:33-45` uses `ApplicationContextRunner` with the real `AdminCredentials` configuration. It shows that a bad password fails startup, names `ADMIN_PASSWORD` and the limit, and never prints the value. That failure is the only step between the policy and the non-zero exit, and nothing in this code base intercepts it. The finding itself says Spring Boot "normally exits non-zero on context failure", and `tasks.md` 2.2 records the context-level check as the intended mechanism. So no wrong behaviour exists in this code; at most there is an optional extra process-level smoke check, which is a documentation preference rather than a correctness defect.

Refuted: the scenario can't actually happen. No user or attacker can get the backend to serve requests with a short ADMIN_PASSWORD, and nothing can make it exit with status 0.

How startup works:
- `AdminCredentials` (src/main/kotlin/cz/doucko/admin/application/AdminCredentials.kt) is an eager singleton `@Component`. Its `hash` initializer throws `AdminPasswordRefusedException` (an `IllegalStateException`) while the bean is being constructed, whenever the password policy reports a violation.
- I searched src/main for `@Lazy` and `lazy-initialization` and found no matches, so the bean is created during context refresh, before the web server accepts requests.
- `main` is a plain `runApplication<DouckoBackendApplication>(*args)` (DouckoBackendApplication.kt:10). There is no custom `SpringApplication` setup, no `exitProcess`, and no try/catch around it.
- Standard Spring Boot behaviour: `SpringApplication.run` reports the failure, closes the context and re-throws. The exception escapes `main`, and the JVM exits non-zero.

So "context fails to start" leads directly to "process exits non-zero before serving any request" through framework behaviour, not through any project code. AdminStartupTest.kt:33 tests the refusal itself: startup fails, the message names ADMIN_PASSWORD and the limit, and the password value is never shown.

What's left of the finding is a note about how the evidence is documented (no process-level smoke test records the exit code). It isn't a defect anyone could reproduce. The reviewer also gave it low confidence and admits Spring Boot normally exits non-zero. At most it's a one-line note for design.md, not a real spec-compliance gap.
